reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a trading robot with an estimated daily revenue of 0.35 USDT after paying 2.1 USDT and directs viewers to register through an external site. It demonstrates depositing cryptocurrency through a TRC20 wallet, entering a transaction ID, and uploading payment proof to activate the robot. The content is a direct solicitation for money and account registration rather than reporting, criticism, or neutral investment analysis.

opening.argument: Judge, the revenue figure is presented as an estimate, not a guaranteed payout: the speaker calls it “estimated for daily revenue,” and the purchase screen labels it “Estimated Daily Revenue” while also displaying a warning prompt. That distinction matters. The video shows a projected figure alongside purchase terms and a visible risk notice, not proof that the creator promises viewers a certain return. The more grounded reading is an explanation of what this trading tool displays.

citations.quote: every year 2.1 is estimated for daily revenue that is, 0.35 USDT

rebuttal.rebuttal: The registration link and recharge instructions establish that viewers can follow the process, but they do not turn an explicitly estimated figure into a guaranteed return. The cited purchase screen includes both the estimate and a warning prompt. The opening also does not identify a statement that any viewer actually earned the displayed amount.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling revenue “estimated” does not erase the central pitch: the speaker connects renting a robot for 2.1 USDT to estimated daily revenue of 0.35 USDT, then walks viewers through recharging an account. The warning prompt does not change the practical effect of directing viewers toward payment for a purported income-producing robot.

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker repeatedly frames this as a walkthrough: “I will now show you how to recharge your account,” then explains how to upload a payment screenshot and use the recharge control. The same procedural approach continues when the speaker checks the robot warehouse and explains account activation. Those are demonstrations of interface steps, not evidence that a trade succeeded or that a return was paid. The video can be understood as an operational tutorial about a trading-robot site, even though the interface includes paid options.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies registration, TRC20 recharge, and activation steps. But those same details are the subject of the demonstration; their presence alone does not show a completed payment or realized profit. The speaker describes what to click and says the robot warehouse shows zero robots, a limited observation that the solicitation reading does not address.

citations.quote: So we click here to send us my account Check my robot warehouse So now the data says zero robots
I will now show you how to recharge your account I will now show you how to use TRC20

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A tutorial can also be promotional. Here the walkthrough tells viewers to register, recharge through TRC20, activate an account, and rent a robot associated with estimated daily revenue. The fact that payment or profit is not shown as completed does not make those instructions neutral; they guide viewers through the steps needed to participate.

opening.argument: Judge, this could be read as a demonstration of a paid service, not proof of fraud. The interface shows a robot contract with a price, a tradeable amount, and an estimated daily revenue figure; the site also offers ordinary account-service controls, including help and withdrawal options. A deposit workflow is plainly shown, so the defense need not deny it. What the supplied material does not establish is a guaranteed payout, a completed purchase, or a failed withdrawal. A registration link and instructions for buying a service deserve scrutiny, but they do not by themselves establish those missing outcomes.

citations.quote: edaibot link https://www.edaitrade.com/#/register?code=27101987

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening establishes a real payment path and an estimated income figure; neither should be minimized. Its stronger conclusion, however, depends on treating that estimate as a deceptive promise. The purchase screen presents a priced contract and labels revenue as estimated, while the visible service menu includes withdrawal and help controls. Those controls do not prove the service works, but the cited material also does not show that it fails.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The missing proof of a failed withdrawal is not the decisive issue. The video supplies a registration link, demonstrates a crypto recharge form requiring a transaction ID and payment screenshot, and ties a priced robot contract to estimated daily revenue. Help and withdrawal buttons do not verify that withdrawals work. Taken together, the demonstrated payment path and income claim support treating this as promotion of a trading-bot returns scheme.
